DAMS & RAIN: The Perfect Storm

By: Anina Peens | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As water levels are rising in the Orange and Vaal river systems, so are fears of possible flooding. If more rain is expected in March, can it result in a flood?

Unique Selling Point:
The effects of Cyclone Eloise were felt in provinces like Mpumalange and Kwa Zulu Natal, but what does this massive influx of water and high rainfall mean for the Northern Cape dams and rivers? Is a flood looming and are we ready to handle it?

Summary:
Dams across the country are slowly filling up. South Africa’s two largest dams, the Gariep and Vanderkloof dams have reached full capacity while the Vaal dam has risen with 5% since last week and is currently at 80%. Fear and anxiety about a possible flood are on the rise, not only amongst those living around dams and rivers and in low-lying areas, but also in the agricultural and tourism sector, especially in South Africa’s largest province the Northern Cape. Here, a six-year drought has been broken by the heavy rains that came as a result of cyclone Eloise that hit Mozambique two weeks ago. The question is, is South Africa ready to face a possible flood? Some say, it is already too late, while others feel there is no need for panic, yet.

Further information:
Background

Social media is hype with photos and videos of South Africans traveling to see the massive release of water at South Africa’s largest dams. The close to 3000 cumecs per second of water, flowing over the walls of the Gariep and Vanderkloof dam have social media talking. But while it may be visually fascinating at face value, anxiety about a possible flood comparable to 1988 and 2011, is a reality for many. These are people living and working around and on the longest river in South Africa, the Orange.

1. Water Management

If a flood in the Orange river systems occurs, water levels can rise to a volume four times bigger than the dam’s capacity. Therefore, some say that water should have been released from the systems by opening the sluices before the cyclone made landfall. They say that it is too late now, and that a flood is inevitable. But other experts disagree and say that water is being managed by highly competent engineers who know what they are doing.

- We explore this: how is water managed during heavy rains, especially in light of forecasts that South Africa may see even more rain in March that may continue until May.
- When do you open a sluice and why are they not open at Vanderkloof? Because if the Vaal pushes up more, it will have to release and when Vanderkloof and Gariep release at the same time, a flood is unavoidable.

2. Agriculture

- Will the result of corruption lead to possible devastation? After the 2011 floods, government rolled out plans to prevent the mass destruction of farms in the lower Orange region where massive commercial farms operate, creating thousands of jobs for the poverty-stricken local community. To prevent devastation of future floods, government secured just under a billion Rand to build flood walls between Vryburg and Upington and lower lying areas such as Kakamas and Keimoes. But the money disappeared, and the walls were never built. With a potential flood looming, corruption may be the cause of mass devastation and possible loss of lives.

- Those at the biggest risk of a possible flood are sustenance farmers and small business owners of tourism spots close to riverbanks. It is a rule of thumb that a drought will always be followed by a flood. Since a drought had the Northern Cape in a grip for nearly 7 years, many people moved closer to water. What happens now? The formal agricultural sector updates their farming network with information and warnings every three hours, but this communication does not reach the small-scale farmers and communities on the water.

3. Tourism

- River rafting in South Africa is big. People book river rafting holidays more than a year in advance. The season for rafting starts in March and ends in May. In the Lower Orange river area, more than 20 river rafting companies create employment and add to the local economy during this period. But the entire season is cancelled this year and the potential loss of income to the area is estimated at R30million Rand.

• Can government be blamed for poor management affecting these industries or are they doing what they can to prevent the perfect storm?

Reason for legal: Certain allegations are being made suggesting that the National department of water affairs were not maintaining flood sluices at Vanderkloof Dam. Further to this, a dam in Cookwas was set to be built 8 years ago but the money allocated for the dam allegedly disappeared. It is also alleged that 1 billion Rand that was allocated for the erection of flood walls in the lower Orange areas such as Upington, disappeared and that the walls were never built.

Reason for graphics: the story needs a map to explain the Vaal and Orange system and what can possibly happen in a flood.

Script:


The Perfect Storm FINAL

INTRO (visual)
VO
As a result of cyclone Eloise that hit Mozambique mid-January, large parts of the country experienced above average rainfall. Although Eloise mostly effected Mpumalanga, Limpopo and Kwa-Zulu Natal, the rain resulting from the storm.
This filled up the Vaal/Orange integrated river systems and the country’s largest dams in the Northern Cape, Free State and North West Provinces.
The full dams created spectacular sights in the usually arid Northern Cape while the rain brought colour to the landscapes that have been released from the grip of a six-year long drought.

VO
By mid-February the Northern Cape received an average rainfall of 300mm in some places and social media was buzzing with photos of waterfalls, full rivers, dams and streams.

VO
The high water resulted in the opening of sluices at the Vaaldam to make space for more water.

LINK
PLEASE CUT AND OVERLAY THIS LINK FOR BRONWYN FOR SOCIAL MEDIA?
I am standing on the Vaal where the water is flowing at 130 per second… it is spectacular…”

VO
But while the high rainfall has many excited, it has others worried as more rain can lead to floods. Climatology Professor Francois Engelbrecht says, despite Cyclone Eloise, a second tropical storm hit Mozambique after Eloise and more storms are likely this year.

Please cut so he can say just this
SUPER@ PROF. FRANCOIS ENGELBRECHT, CLIMATOLOGIST, WITS
“We are experiencing a season with tropical weather systems forming in the Mozambique channel, that is something that doesn’t happen every year.
BACK-TO-BACK
“These systems can cause catastrophic flooding and in some cases flash flooding. The problem is that they can bring 100 to 300 mm of rain in the span of a few days”

LINK
Over the last ten years, we have seen an increase in tropical storms as a result of Global warming the risk here is not really the frequency at which these storms occur but the intensity with which they occur.

VO
Adding more water to already saturated dams, rivers and soil has many concerned over government’s flood readiness plan.

SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, AGRISA
19’40”-19’53”
“The flooding is already happening, the big challenge for us is to make sure that the flooding does not get worse…”

VO
Executive director of Agri SA, Christo van der Rheede says, organized agriculture has been in continues communication with government after many farms, especially in the lower Catchment area of the Orange river already flooded as a result of the cyclone.
PLEASE CUT AND OVERLAY THIS BYTE FOR BRONWYN FOR SOCIAL MEDIA?
SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, AGRI SA
5’14”-5’38”
“If they predict a lot of rain then the dam managers will normally release water before it causes major damage, because there is no use you wait until the dam is entirely filled up and now you have to release water on a big scale. That leads to serious problems lower down the river system.

VO
The Vaal and Orange river catchment area covers 48% percent of South Africa’s surface. And not only are farmers in these areas on high alert, but many players in the tourism sector are losing out on an entire season of river-based tourism. Packing up his adventure camp amidst of the fully booked high season at Onseepkans on the Orange river in the Northern Cape, Andrew Keller says, he is facing a loss of income of more than 2 million Rand

PLEASE CUT SO HE CAN SAY JUST WHAT IS WRITTEN HERE?
SUPER@ ANDREW KELLER, BUSINESS OWNER, ONSEEPKANS, N. CAPE
“As you can see behind me, the camp is pretty flooded at the moment. So, I personally think this could have been avoided by pre-releases.

VO
Keller’s counterparts on the Vaal river also cancelled various trips.

PROF GRAEME ADDISSON,(PLEASE CHECK, ONE S) BUSINESS OWNER, VAAL RIVER
05’04”-05’41”
“Perhaps if they know a lot of water is coming into the dam, the time to open some of the gates is earlier, when the flow can still be controlled and when the dam is at 80-85% they can let a lot of that water go because there is more water coming in.”

VO
Professor Graeme Addison has been operating a river rafting business on the Vaal for 20 years.

PROF GRAEME ADDISSON, BUSINESS OWNER, VAAL RIVER
O2’14”-03’05”
“The danger on this river is as you can see there are a lot of trees and for a person to get into one of those trees is bad news. So, we stop rafting at 850 cumecs”

VO (INSERT AMATEUR RESCUE VIDEO, CREDIT: COURTESY GRAEME ADDISON)
Water flow is measured in cumecs. 1 cumec equals a thousand litres of water per cubic meter…per second. This means a flow of 8 and a half million litres a second… way too fast for river rafting, especially for amateurs. But Addison says the rising water levels from the open sluices attracted many thrill-seekers … and rescue operations had to be performed.

LINK PLEASE CUT AND OVERLAY THIS LINK FOR BRONWYN FOR SOCIAL MEDIA?
“Rivers and dams are raising exponentially and while some people may wait for the water levels to rise for a fun day out on the river, safety instructors warn that people should not underestimate the rivers as currents change drastically during high water levels and floods.

VO
With more rainfall expected, increased water volumes are not only dangerous for rafters but farmers fear a repeat of the floods of 2011 and at worst, the flood of 1988.
A farmer from the Upington area says he was 11 years old when the 1988 floods occurred.

SUPER@ WILCO FOURIE, FARMER, UPINGTON
“I remember that we went to bed after the first water came into our lands, and waking up the next morning, everything was under water. So that was very scary site to see, and after the flood waters was gone and we could go back into the vineyards, I would never forget the look on my dad’s face when he saw all the destruction that was caused by the flood.

VO HIER SOEK HULLE N GRAFIEK. EK STUUR VIR JOU N EMAIL OP WORD MET WAT HULLE BEDOEL
In 1988 the Orange river reached peaks of 7400 cumecs per second. That means nearly seven and a half million liters of water flowed per second past a specific point.
The highest peak the Orange river reached so far this year was just below 3000 cumecs.
Fourie says although the Vaal dam sluices were opened, Gariep and Vanderkloof dams should have been opened before they reached full capacity.

SUPER@ WILCO FOURIE, FARMER, UPINGTON (ONS KAN DIE BYTE DROP AS ONS MOET TYD OPMAAK, DAN MOET JY NET ‘N CUTAWAY SIT VAN CLAIRE EN WILCO EN N CLOSE UP VAN WILCO OOR DIE LAASTE SIN HIERBO WAT ONDERSTREEP IS)
“We asked for something similar about a month ago in the Orange river also to create space for the rain that is coming”

VO
The department of Water and Sanitations says the decision to release water from the Vaaldam was done as precaution to prevent floods lower downstream in the wake of the second tropical storm (take out)

SUPER@SPUTNIK RATAU, DEPT. WATER & SANITATION
“We released water from the Vaal dam into the Bloemhof dam and into the Northern Cape so that we can bring relief to the Vaaldam and to make way for the expected inflows from the activity coming through the Mozambican channel.”

VO
If a flood occurs, another major concern for farmers around the lower Orange river catchment areas, is the collapse of flood walls, erected to protect close to 30 thousand hectares of farmland.

SUPER@ CHRISTO VAN DER RHEEDE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, AGRI SA
2’28”-3’19” (KAN ONS SY UHMS AND AAHS UITSNY? HY SUKKEL VREESLIK OM BY DIE PUNT UIT TE KOM)
“These flood walls were erected in the 1950’s by the then department of Agriculture. And we have requested the department of Agriculture to make money available so that we could maintain those walls and also increase the height of some of those walls and in some areas to rebuild the walls. That was after the 2011 floods that we experienced. The department made approximately one point two billion Rand available. But we have now discovered that most of that money was spent but there was approximately 300 million that was still left.”

VO
The Northern Cape department of Agriculture says all the work was completed. But farmers say there are gaps of 70km that occur in the 400 km long flood walls.

SUPER@ WILCO FOURIE, FARMER
“So a chain is only as strong as the weakest link. So if there is a gap and the water goes in, you will have water behind the wall and that will cause a lot of damage.”

VO
In a written reply the Northern Cape MEC of Agriculture, Mase Manopole, said a team of her department’s engineers were instructed to inspect the flood walls.

LINK
“Manopole stated that the funds were utilized and that they upgraded the walls. She added that outstanding walls were in areas that we not initially surveyed hence there was no costing attached to them and that the walls are also the responsibility of the landowners”

VO
Raisin farms around the lower Orange river contribute nearly 2 billion Rand to the GDP, creating more than 30 thousand jobs. (KAN JY DALK DAAI CLIP TERUGSIT VAN DIE WERKERS WAT DRUIWE PLUK?)

VO
Farmers will rely heavily on early water releases as the flood walls are unlikely to hold during a flood.

SUPER@ SPUTNIK RATAU, DEPT. WATER & SANITATION
“We are on alert that more rain is expected and those warnings that have come in could cause floods. That is why we have to manage our infrastructure and manage how much water is coming into our infrastructure in order to take away the risk of the flood.”

VO
Danie van der Spuy retired at the end of January after he spent his life as specialist engineer in flood studies for the national department of water and sanitation.

SUPER@DANIE VAN DER SPUY, FORMER SPECIALIST ENGINEER, DEPT OF WATER AFFAIRS
“I don’t think people should be too worried about what is going on at Water Affairs. There are people with knowledge at Water affairs and they know what they are doing. We rely on instruments and flow measurements.”

VO
For 27 years Van der Spuy was the man making the decisions on when to open the sluices at the country’s main dams.

CLAIRE TO DANIE
“Some people are concerned they say that water should have been released from the dams already, what would you say to that?

SUPER@DANIE VAN DER SPUY, FORMER SPECIALIST ENGINEER, DEPT. WATER & SANITATION
9’02”- 9’42”
“You can’t create a flood downstream that is bigger than the flood that enters the dam, in other words you cannot create a flood that is bigger than the natural one

VO
Protecting the integrity of the dam walls, ensuring the safety of people and maintaining the dam levels at 100% are all priorities when managing water, says Van der Spuy. He added that it has never been necessary to open sluices at the Gariep or Vanderkloof dams.

LINK
The Vaal dam and the Bloemhof dam are both earth filled embankments with controlled water release… the Gariep and Vanderkloof dam are concrete structures…..”

VO
And although 6 sluices at the Vaal dam were opened, taking the risk of opening more sluices can result in empty dams if the rain doesn't come. – END -

2’47”-3’13”
SUPER@DANIE VAN DER SPUY, FORMER SPECIALIST ENGINEER, DEPT OF WATER AFFAIRS
“We don’t anticipate floods, if the weather bureau issues a warning of higher rainfall that might happen, we still can’t react on that, I can’t react on things that are not physical. We start reacting when we see the rain is falling and we see flow in the river. That is the only way in which we can operate these dams”


Promos

It has been a wet year so far, and if forecasters are correct, it is going to get even wetter. While this may excite some people, it has others worried about the state’s flood preparedness plan and whether the country is ready for a flood.

Fearing a repeat of a flood similar to the floods of 2011, some say government should already have opened sluices amidst the above average rainfall the country has experienced.

While there are forecasts of more rain this summer, we take a look at water management in South Africa and how water is controlled during high rainfall periods.

SUPER@DANIE VAN DER SPUY, FORMER SPECIALIST ENGINEER, DEPT OF WATER AFFAIRS “I don’t think people should be too worried about what is going on at Water Affairs. CLAIRE TO DANIE “Some people are concerned they say that water should have been released from the dams already, what would you say to that? SUPER@DANIE VAN DER SPUY, FORMER SPECIALIST ENGINEER, DEPT. WATER & SANITATION 9’02”- 9’42” “You can’t create a flood downstream that is bigger than the flood that enters the dam, in other words you cannot create a flood that is bigger than the natural one VO Protecting the integrity of the dam walls, ensuring the safety of people and maintaining the dam levels at 100% are all priorities when managing water, says Van der Spuy. He added that it has never been necessary to open sluices at the Gariep or Vanderkloof dams. LINK The Vaal dam and the Bloemhof dam are both earth filled embankments with controlled water release… the Gariep and Vanderkloof dam are concrete structures…..” VO And although 6 sluices at the Vaal dam were opened, taking the risk of opening more sluices can result in empty dams if the rain doesn't come. – END - 2’47”-3’13” SUPER@DANIE VAN DER SPUY, FORMER SPECIALIST ENGINEER, DEPT OF WATER AFFAIRS “We don’t anticipate floods, if the weather bureau issues a warning of higher rainfall that might happen, we still can’t react on that, I can’t react on things that are not physical. We start reacting when we see the rain is falling and we see flow in the river. That is the only way in which we can operate these dams” Promos It has been a wet year so far, and if forecasters are correct, it is going to get even wetter. While this may excite some people, it has others worried about the state’s flood preparedness plan and whether the country is ready for a flood. Fearing a repeat of a flood similar to the floods of 2011, some say government should already have opened sluices amidst the above average rainfall the country has experienced. While there are forecasts of more rain this summer, we take a look at water management in South Africa and how water is controlled during high rainfall periods.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): As water levels are rising in the Orange and Vaal river systems, so are fears of possible flooding. If more rain is expected in March, can it result in a flood?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The effects of Cyclone Eloise were felt in provinces like Mpumalange and Kwa Zulu Natal, but what does this massive influx of water and high rainfall mean for the Northern Cape dams and rivers? Is a flood looming and are we ready to handle it?
metadata.Summary: Dams across the country are slowly filling up. South Africa’s two largest dams, the Gariep and Vanderkloof dams have reached full capacity while the Vaal dam has risen with 5% since last week and is currently at 80%. Fear and anxiety about a possible flood are on the rise, not only amongst those living around dams and rivers and in low-lying areas, but also in the agricultural and tourism sector, especially in South Africa’s largest province the Northern Cape. Here, a six-year drought has been broken by the heavy rains that came as a result of cyclone Eloise that hit Mozambique two weeks ago. The question is, is South Africa ready to face a possible flood? Some say, it is already too late, while others feel there is no need for panic, yet.
metadata.Further information: Background Social media is hype with photos and videos of South Africans traveling to see the massive release of water at South Africa’s largest dams. The close to 3000 cumecs per second of water, flowing over the walls of the Gariep and Vanderkloof dam have social media talking. But while it may be visually fascinating at face value, anxiety about a possible flood comparable to 1988 and 2011, is a reality for many. These are people living and working around and on the longest river in South Africa, the Orange. 1. Water Management If a flood in the Orange river systems occurs, water levels can rise to a volume four times bigger than the dam’s capacity. Therefore, some say that water should have been released from the systems by opening the sluices before the cyclone made landfall. They say that it is too late now, and that a flood is inevitable. But other experts disagree and say that water is being managed by highly competent engineers who know what they are doing. - We explore this: how is water managed during heavy rains, especially in light of forecasts that South Africa may see even more rain in March that may continue until May. - When do you open a sluice and why are they not open at Vanderkloof? Because if the Vaal pushes up more, it will have to release and when Vanderkloof and Gariep release at the same time, a flood is unavoidable. 2. Agriculture - Will the result of corruption lead to possible devastation? After the 2011 floods, government rolled out plans to prevent the mass destruction of farms in the lower Orange region where massive commercial farms operate, creating thousands of jobs for the poverty-stricken local community. To prevent devastation of future floods, government secured just under a billion Rand to build flood walls between Vryburg and Upington and lower lying areas such as Kakamas and Keimoes. But the money disappeared, and the walls were never built. With a potential flood looming, corruption may be the cause of mass devastation and possible loss of lives. - Those at the biggest risk of a possible flood are sustenance farmers and small business owners of tourism spots close to riverbanks. It is a rule of thumb that a drought will always be followed by a flood. Since a drought had the Northern Cape in a grip for nearly 7 years, many people moved closer to water. What happens now? The formal agricultural sector updates their farming network with information and warnings every three hours, but this communication does not reach the small-scale farmers and communities on the water. 3. Tourism - River rafting in South Africa is big. People book river rafting holidays more than a year in advance. The season for rafting starts in March and ends in May. In the Lower Orange river area, more than 20 river rafting companies create employment and add to the local economy during this period. But the entire season is cancelled this year and the potential loss of income to the area is estimated at R30million Rand. • Can government be blamed for poor management affecting these industries or are they doing what they can to prevent the perfect storm?
